targets.title: How guilt and pride shape subsequent self-control.
targets.evidence_quote: In addition to conducting a replication study of Hofmann and Fisher (2012), we also examined the following three hypotheses.
targets.outcome_quote: Comparison of these results with those of Hofmann and Fisher's (2012) study on thematic self-control revealed that previous guilt had beneficial indirect pathways on subsequent self-control processes (goal importance, conflict, and resistance) to inhibit desire-related behavior. However, the latter reported that guilt for self-control failures had detrimental residual effects on subsequent behavioral inhibition, whereas the former did not demonstrate such a negative effect. Furthermore, although Hofmann and Fisher (2012) found that previous pride had beneficial indirect pathways on subsequent self-control processes, this study found no positive impact of pride on self-control processes.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors report agreement for beneficial indirect guilt effects, but contrast the absence of detrimental residual guilt and beneficial pride effects with the original. No overall successful verdict overrides these comparisons.
